files.lesson.md: --- order: 4 unit: rules node: AC9M7A04 n1 uses: [AC9M7N07 n1] # reads −6 °C off a temperature axis title: Reading a graph summary: A point on a graph of real data pairs two measurements. Find one value on its axis, go to the line, and read across to the other axis. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Weather maps, phone battery meters and sports stats all use graphs. Before you can use one, you need to read it: which number is on which axis?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8148 url: http://127.0.0.1:8148/index.html readySelector: "#sl-cursor" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: data.yml#pic, caption: "At 15 hours the temperature is 24 °C: find 15 on the Time axis, go up to the line, read across to the Temperature axis. The point is $(15, 24)$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@data.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Find one value, go to the line, read the other" say: "Find one value on its axis, go to the line, read the other." clip: - caption: { text: "Time is across. Temperature is up.", say: "Time is along the bottom. Temperature is up the side." } - wait: 400 - click: Move the cursor right - click: Move the cursor right - click: Move the cursor right - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "At 9 h, go up to the line: 14 °C.", say: "At nine hours, go up to the line: fourteen degrees." } - expect: { selector: "#gread", contains: "Temperature = 14 °C" } - click: Move the cursor right - click: Move the cursor right - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "At 15 h it is 24 °C: the point (15, 24).", say: "At fifteen hours it is twenty-four degrees: the point fifteen, twenty-four." } - expect: { selector: "#gread", contains: "Temperature = 24 °C" } - wait: 1200 connection: daylight-hours --- A graph of real data pairs two measurements. Each point says: **when this one was measured, that one was measured**. To read a graph, first check the **axis labels**: what is measured across, and what is measured up. The data on these graphs are made up for the task. ## Predict: what does a point say? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to what (15, 24) means exposes swapped axes and reading the point as one number, before any graph is shown." check: type: predict q: "A graph shows temperature (°C) up the side and time (h) along the bottom. One point on it is $(15, 24)$. What does that point say?" options: ["At 15 hours the temperature is 24 °C", "At 24 hours the temperature is 15 °C", "The temperature went up by 15, then by 24", "It is 15 °C for 24 hours"] actual: "At 15 hours the temperature is 24 °C. The first number is read along the bottom axis (Time), the second up the side (Temperature), just as when you plotted points. (At 24 hours the temperature is 15 °C swaps the axes.)" ``` Which axis is the first number read from? What are the units of each number? ## Run: move the cursor ```step stage: run insight: "Moving the cursor along the line shows both readings change together: the time on the bottom axis and the temperature at the line." try: { playground: board, starter: "data.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "Move the cursor $R$ to 15 hours. Was your prediction right?", when: "x(R) = 15" } ``` Use the slider, the − and + buttons, or click on the graph. The readout names both values with their units. At 15 hours, how hot is it? ## Investigate: reading values ```step stage: investigate insight: "Reading a graph is four moves: check the axes, find the known value on its own axis, go to the line, read across to the other axis; the units go in the answer. Swapping the axes is the common slip." tasks: - picture: { ref: data.yml#temp-plain, caption: "Temperature (°C) over one day. Time (h) is along the bottom." } check: type: answer q: "What is the temperature at 9 hours?" answer: "14" feedback: - ["9", "That is the time you were given. Go up from 9 on the Time axis to the line, then read across to the Temperature axis."] - ["12", "Check the gridlines: the line at 9 h is between 10 and 15."] explain: "At 9 h the line is at 14 °C, so the point is (9, 14)." - picture: { ref: data.yml#temp-plain, caption: "The same graph." } check: type: answer q: "At what time (in hours) is the temperature highest?" answer: "15" feedback: - ["24", "24 is the highest temperature, read up the side. The question asks for the time, read along the bottom."] explain: "The highest point is (15, 24): the temperature is highest at 15 h." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#priya" text: "Priya reads the temperature at 6 hours from the graph. Click the line where she goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: axes-swapped explain: "Line 4: the line is at 9 when the time is 6, and 9 is read up the side, so it is the temperature. At 6 hours the temperature is 9 °C. Priya swapped the two numbers." ``` ### Temperature Here is how to read a graph, step by step. ```worked \text{Axes: Time (h) across, Temperature (°C) up} :: Check the labels first. \text{Time} = 9 \text{ h} :: Find the value you know on its own axis. (9, \; ?) :: Go up from 9 to the line. \text{Temperature} = 14 \text{ °C} :: Read across to the other axis. \text{At 9 h the temperature is 14 °C.} :: Say it in a sentence, with the units. ``` ### The highest point ### Find the mistake Read Priya's working one line at a time. Which number came from which axis? ## Modify: other graphs ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: read the other way (from the up-axis to the across-axis), a flat section, and negative values below the axis." try: { playground: board, starter: "data.yml#fuel", height: 560 } tasks: - starter: "data.yml#fuel" hint: "Read up the side to find 26, then follow across to the line." check: { type: board, text: "A car's fuel tank: fuel (L) against distance (km). Move $R$ to where 26 litres are left. How far has it gone?", when: "y(R) = 26", explain: "The line is at 26 L when the distance is 200 km: the point is (200, 26)." } - picture: { ref: data.yml#plant-plain, caption: "A plant's height (cm) week by week." } check: type: question q: "What happens to the plant's height from week 3 to week 6?" options: ["It increases", "It decreases", "It stays the same (a flat line)"] answer: 2 explain: "The line is flat from week 3 to week 6: the height is 14 cm each time, so it does not change." - picture: { ref: data.yml#night-plain, caption: "Temperature (°C) through a winter night. Below the axis is below zero." } hint: "A point below the Time axis has a negative temperature." check: type: answer q: "What is the lowest temperature on the night graph, in °C?" answer: "-6" feedback: - ["6", "The lowest point is below the axis, so the temperature is negative."] explain: "The lowest point is (8, −6): at 8 hours the temperature is −6 °C." ``` ### Fuel Each task loads a new graph. Read the axis labels first. ### A flat line ### Below zero ## Practise: read the graph ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading both ways on new graphs, mixed with a sentence-meaning question so students must decide which axis each number comes from; the review is substitution from an earlier lesson." tasks: - picture: { ref: data.yml#temp-plain, caption: "Temperature (°C) over one day." } check: type: answer q: "What is the temperature at 21 hours?" answer: "16" feedback: - ["21", "That is the time. Read the temperature up the side."] explain: "At 21 h the line is at 16 °C: the point is (21, 16)." - picture: { ref: data.yml#fuel-plain, caption: "Fuel (L) against distance (km)." } check: type: answer q: "How much fuel is left after 300 km, in litres?" answer: "14" feedback: - ["300", "That is the distance. The fuel is read up the side."] explain: "At 300 km the line is at 14 L: the point is (300, 14)." - check: type: question q: "A graph of cost ($) against time (hours) has the point $(4, 30)$. Which sentence is true?" options: ["4 hours cost $30", "30 hours cost $4", "The cost went up by $4 over 30 hours"] answer: 0 explain: "The first number is the time (4 hours) and the second is the cost ($30)." - check: type: answer q: "Review: find $y = 4x + 1$ when $x = 3$." answer: "13" feedback: - ["43", "4x means 4 × x, not 4 then 3."] explain: "y = 4 × 3 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13." ``` ### The time ### The fuel ### Which sentence? ### Review ## Make: tell a story with a graph ```step stage: make insight: "Making a graph from a story reverses reading: students choose each value to fit the words." try: { playground: board, starter: "data.yml#make", height: 560 } hint: ["The battery starts full. What is the battery at 0 hours?", "Each point must be lower than the one before it, and the last one is 20."] check: { type: board, text: "Mia's phone is fully charged (100%) at 0 hours. It goes down every two hours, and is at 20% after 8 hours. Drag each point up or down to draw it.", when: "y(A) = 100 and y(B) < y(A) and y(C) < y(B) and y(D) < y(C) and y(E) = 20", explain: "Start at 100 and end at 20, lower each time, such as 100, 80, 60, 40, 20 (a steady fall) or 100, 70, 50, 30, 20." } ``` The points move up and down only. Then answer: what does your graph say about the battery at 4 hours? Stretch: draw a graph where the battery falls quickly at first, then slowly. ## Make: read a daylight graph on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Reading the lowest and highest points of a year graph needs the right axis for each number; the paper task makes them pick the axis for the month." hint: ["Find the lowest point on the line first.", "Read the month along the bottom and the hours up the side."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "This graph of daylight in a town over one year is made up for the task, shaped like a real southern-hemisphere year. Daylight (hours) is up the side and the month number is along the bottom. Its points are $(1, 14)$, $(3, 13)$, $(5, 11)$, $(7, 10)$, $(9, 12)$ and $(11, 14)$. Sketch it on squared paper. How many more hours of daylight does month 1 have than the shortest day's month?" steps: - ["The lowest point is $(7, 10)$", "the shortest daylight is the lowest point on the line"] - ["Month 7 has $10$ hours of daylight", "the first number is the month, the second the hours"] - ["Month 1 has $14$ hours: the point is $(1, 14)$", "read up the side from month 1"] - ["$14 - 10 = 4$", "take the smaller from the larger"] - ["Month 1 has $4$ more hours of daylight", "say it in a sentence, with units"] picks: - step: 2 q: "In the lowest point (7, 10), what does the 7 tell you?" options: - "It is month 7 (read along the bottom)" - "There are 7 hours of daylight" - "The line has gone down 7" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Hours are read up the side. The 10 is the hours.", "The first number is a position along the bottom axis, not a drop."] answer: "4" feedback: - ["10", "That is the hours of daylight at the lowest point. Take it away from the hours in month 1."] - ["6", "Check: month 1 is 14 hours, not 16."] criteria: - "I labelled the axes: month across, hours of daylight up." - "I read each number from the right axis." - "My answer says '4 more hours', with the unit." explain: "The shortest day is at month 7 (10 hours). Month 1 has 14 hours, so 14 − 10 = 4 more hours." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. Real daylight graphs (sunrise and sunset times for your own town) look just like this, with the highest and lowest points a half-year apart. Sketch the points, mark the lowest, then type your answer. **Also used in** - **Daylight and seasons.** A year of sunrise and sunset times, drawn as a graph, shows the longest and shortest days at its highest and lowest points. - **Weather and temperature.** The same reading skill finds the hottest day or the coldest night. - **Science.** Results graphs are read the same way: first the axes, then the point. ```teacher summary: Students read values from graphs of real data, starting from either axis, and say what a point means in a sentence with units (AC9M7A04, node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 13 min goals: - I can say what a point on a graph of real data means, with units. - I can find a value on one axis and read the matching value from the other. - I can tell the graph's variables from its axis labels. struggle: Knowing which number comes from which axis. Students read the point as one number, or take the time as the temperature. Ask them to say each reading as a sentence with units. before: > Do the Run board and the Make board yourself first. The cursor reads both values off the line; students can click the graph, use the slider, or use the − and + buttons. The data are plausible examples, not real measurements. If you have real data (a school weather station, a class experiment), swap in a graph of your own for the Investigate questions. Students know how to plot points (the last lesson). The new move is reading a point as two measurements with units: the first from the bottom axis, the second up the side. Axis labels now carry the names and units, such as Time (h). The Modify tasks read the other way (from the up-axis to the across-axis), meet a flat section, and meet negative values below the axis. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Ask a student who chose 'At 24 hours the temperature is 15 °C' which axis they read first." - "Run: ask students to say each reading in a sentence with units before moving the cursor." - "Investigate: model the worked example live on a projected graph: say the axes, put a finger on the known value, go to the line, then across." - "Modify: before the fuel graph, ask: which axis is the 26 on?" - "Make: compare two students' graphs. Both fall every two hours. How do they differ?" - "Paper: the daylight graph is sketched in books from the given points; the page marks the 4 hours and that the 7 is a month, read along the bottom. Books out, then compare sketches." stuck: - see: A student gives the time when asked for the temperature, or the reverse (Priya's mistake). ask: What is this axis called? Is 9 measured in hours or in degrees? fix: "Write the units next to each number: 6 h and 9 °C. Then say the sentence: at 6 hours the temperature is 9 °C." - see: A student cannot find a value between gridlines. ask: Which two gridlines is the line between? Is it closer to the lower or the upper one? fix: Count the grid squares in fives or tens, and use the cursor's readout to check. - see: A student reads a negative value as positive. ask: Is the point above or below the Time axis? fix: "Below the axis is below zero: write the minus sign." stretch: Using the temperature graph, find two different times when the temperature is 16 °C. Why are there two? support: Give a printed graph with the gridlines labelled and a ruler, and read the first value together, naming the axis out loud. leads: > Next: describing the whole relationship in words (it increases, decreases or stays constant) instead of one point at a time. Where it leads in class: reading graphs in science experiments and in geography. exit: q: A graph of height (cm) against age (years) has the point (12, 150). What does it say? a: At 12 years the height is 150 cm. explain: > A graph of real data pairs two measurements. Check the **axis labels** first: one measurement is across (the bottom axis) and the other is up the side. To read a graph, find the value you know on its own axis, go to the line, then read across to the other axis. The point $(15, 24)$ on a graph of temperature against time says: at 15 hours the temperature is 24 °C. Give the units in your answer. The two numbers of a point belong to different axes. Swapping them gives a different (and wrong) statement. ```
